name: Sec-Fetch-* request metadata
plain: Browsers add headers saying where a request came from and why, which servers use to block cross-site abuse.
meaning: Sec-Fetch-Site, Mode, Dest and User tell the server if a request is same-origin, a navigation, or user triggered. They are not user identifying but help servers tell real browsers from scripts.

limits.headline: Can tell why a request was sent, such as a click or a script
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser adds it to every request automatically
can: See whether a request came from the same site, another site, or from you directly
See whether it came from a click, a typed address or a page script
Block suspicious cross site requests and bots that lack the right labels
cannot: See your name, location or account from these labels
Be changed by the page, since the browser sets them
Learn which other pages you visited

story.what_it_is: Browsers label each request with where it came from and why, so servers can reject cross site abuse.

marketing.name: Fetch Metadata
marketing.pitch: Servers can use these labels to block requests that are not meant for them, as a defence against many web attacks.

story.for_you: You never see these labels, but they help protect you. They let sites refuse a request that a hostile page secretly sent using your logged in session.
story.for_makers: Makers add a short rule on the server: only accept some requests from their own pages. It blocks forged requests and data leaks across sites. Because browsers set the labels, a page cannot fake them.

use_cases.example: A bank's server refuses a money transfer sent by another site, because the label says it came from a different site and was not a normal navigation.
A social site only returns private profile data to requests from its own pages, so other sites cannot read it through hidden calls.
A browser game's account server rejects score submissions that do not come from its own game page, which cuts simple cheating by third party scripts.
A web editor such as Google Docs protects document data so other sites cannot load it into a hidden frame.
A streaming site blocks other sites from embedding its video files by checking the destination label.
An engineer adds a middleware that drops cross site requests to private APIs, then watches the logs for blocked probes.
A security team uses the labels to spot probing from a malicious page in the access logs.

technical_bounds: Absent from non-browser clients, making them a bot signal
Cannot be set by page script

value.legit_uses: CSRF and XSSI defense (resource isolation policies)
